short: A Persianate Turco-Mongol state whose culture long outlasted its political unity.
full:
At its height the empire ran from Anatolia and the Caucasus across Iran and Afghanistan to the Syr Darya, held by a Turco-Mongol military elite and administered in Persian by the bureaucratic class of the old Ilkhanid provinces. Its weakness was structural: land was distributed among princes of the house as appanages, so every succession was a civil war. Its strength was patronage. Samarkand under Timur and Herat under Shah Rukh and his wife Gawhar Shad produced the ribbed and blue-tiled architecture, the miniature painting of Bihzad and the poetry of Jami that later scholars call the Timurid renaissance, and that the Safavids, Ottomans and Mughals all copied.

After Shah Rukh's death in 1447 the western provinces went to the Turkmen confederations, and Abu Sa'id, the last ruler to hold most of the empire together, was captured and executed in 1469. What remained was Herat under Husayn Bayqara and a fragmented Transoxiana. Muhammad Shaybani's Uzbeks took Samarkand at the turn of the century and Herat in 1507, ending the dynasty in its homeland.
